title: The Railway Children
author: E. Nesbit
written: c. 1904–05, while Nesbit was living at Well Hall in Eltham, then in Kent
setting: A cottage called Three Chimneys on a bare hillside above a railway line, a canal and an aqueduct, from a cold May to a still, shiny September; with a London suburb behind it, and a courtroom, a prison and a Siberian mine kept off the page
lengthNote: Fourteen titled chapters, about 59,000 words. The father leaves in the first chapter and does not appear again until the second page from the end
openingLine: They were not railway children to begin with.
summary: Two men call at a comfortable suburban villa after dinner, the father is taken away in a cab, and his wife and three children move to a cold cottage in the country and learn to manage on very little. The children fill the gap with the railway: they wave at the 9.15, cadge facts from the porter, stop a train with their torn red petticoats and organise a birthday for a man who does not want charity. Meanwhile their mother writes stories to keep them fed and says nothing about where their father is. The plot everyone remembers is the rescue; the book’s real subject is what the children are not told, and how long Nesbit can keep the reader in the same position.
referenceStyle: chapter, numbered I to XIV as the book numbers them and cited here by Arabic numeral

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of The Railway Children (eBook 1874)
sourceText.note: A transcription of the 1906 book, carrying Nesbit’s dedication to her son Paul Bland and the fourteen chapter titles. Its italics are set as capital letters — WON’T, THINK, UN-friends — and the quotations here follow it without altering the text; its spellings and its double hyphens for dashes are kept too. Its table of contents heads the eighth chapter ‘The amateur fireman’ and the chapter itself ‘The amateur firemen’; the chapter’s own form is used here. C. E. Brock’s twenty plates are not part of the file.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: Serialised in The London Magazine in thirteen instalments from January 1905, then issued as a book by Wells Gardner, Darton with twenty plates by C. E. Brock.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Each is named for its event — Peter’s coal-mine, Saviours of the train, The terrible secret — and the last is called simply The End.

atAGlance.label: Dedication
atAGlance.note: Nesbit’s son, ‘behind whose knowledge of railways my ignorance confidently shelters’. The book most admired for its engines begins by disclaiming the engineering.

atAGlance.label: The withheld fact
atAGlance.note: The sentence is printed once, in a torn scrap of newspaper in the tenth chapter. Peter and Phyllis never learn it, and the reader is told it only when Bobbie is.

structure.label: Chapters 1–2
structure.title: The knock at the door, and Three Chimneys
structure.summary: Two gentlemen are shown into the library after dinner, the father leaves in a cab, and within weeks the family is unpacking by candlelight in a cold house on a hillside. Nesbit gives the reader the exact shape of a catastrophe and withholds its content, so that the move reads as an adventure and also as a fall.

scenes.title: The beginning of things
scenes.summary: Peter’s birthday engine bursts, the two gentlemen call, Ruth is dismissed for hinting, and the family arrives after dark at a house with no supper in it.

scenes.title: Peter’s coal-mine
scenes.summary: The children find the railway, name the trains, and Peter starts taking coal from the station heap until the Station Master catches him and lets him off.

structure.label: Chapters 3–4
structure.title: The Green Dragon and the old gentleman
structure.summary: A clean hand waves back from a first-class carriage, and a habit becomes a friendship. When their mother has influenza the children ask a stranger for what the doctor has ordered, get it, and are told afterwards that they must never do such a thing again.

scenes.title: The old gentleman
scenes.summary: The daily wave to the 9.15; Peter apologises for the coals; the doctor’s list is painted on a sheet and a hamper comes up from the station.

scenes.title: The engine-burglar
scenes.summary: Their mother’s anger and apology, Bobbie’s birthday with its flower map of the railway, and her ride in the cab of a moving engine with a broken toy under her arm.

structure.label: Chapters 5–7
structure.title: The exile, the landslide and the watches
structure.summary: A shabby foreigner with no ticket is found at the station and taken home, and his story — prison, Siberia, a wife lost somewhere in England — is told to the children as something that happens in Russia. A week or two later they stop a train with their petticoats and are given gold watches for it.

scenes.title: Prisoners and captives
scenes.summary: Peter’s stamps identify the stranger as Russian, their mother interprets, and that night she asks the children to pray for all prisoners and captives.

scenes.title: Saviours of the train
scenes.summary: Perks explains party politics, the trees walk down the cutting, and six flags torn from two red flannel petticoats stop the 11.29 twenty yards short of the mound.

scenes.title: For valour
scenes.summary: A presentation at the station, a short speech from Peter, and Bobbie’s real errand: asking the old gentleman to find the Russian’s wife and child, which he does.

structure.label: Chapters 8–9
structure.title: The canal, and what a birthday costs
structure.summary: Two episodes about how help lands on the person helped. Peter refuses to be driven off a public bridge by a bargeman and then pulls the bargeman’s baby out of a burning cabin; and the village subscribes to a birthday for Perks, who will not have it until he learns exactly who gave what and why.

scenes.title: The amateur firemen
scenes.summary: Bill the Bargee takes Peter by the ear; hours later the cabin is alight, Peter carries out Reginald Horace, and the family gains the freedom of the canal.

scenes.title: The pride of Perks
scenes.summary: Fourteen buns marked A. P., a pram from the post-office, and a furious porter who takes it all back when the labels are read aloud.

structure.label: Chapters 10–12
structure.title: The newspaper, and the dark of the tunnel
structure.summary: A pile of old magazines is wrapped in a sheet of newspaper, and Bobbie learns that her father has been convicted of selling State secrets. She tells her mother, keeps it from the others, and then spends a long cold hour in a tunnel holding the hand of an injured boy who does not know any of it.

scenes.title: The terrible secret
scenes.summary: The quarrel over the rake, Peter’s torn foot, and the printed column headed End of the Trial that Bobbie reads at the level-crossing.

scenes.title: The hound in the red jersey
scenes.summary: Mother tells her about the planted letters and the jealous subordinate; Bobbie writes to the old gentleman; the paperchase runs into the tunnel and one hound does not come out.

scenes.title: What Bobbie brought home
scenes.summary: Bobbie stays with Jim in the dark while Peter and Phyllis wake a signalman who has not slept in five days and refuse the two shillings he offers them.

structure.label: Chapters 13–14
structure.title: The grandfather, and the 11.54
structure.summary: Jim’s grandfather turns out to be the old gentleman from the 9.15, who has been working on the case, without telling anyone, since he read about it. The whole train waves at the children one September morning, and a tall pale man gets off the 11.54.

scenes.title: The hound’s grandfather
scenes.summary: Dr Forrest lectures Peter about how to treat his sisters; Mother becomes matron of a hospital with one patient; at the gate the old gentleman tells Bobbie he has hopes.

scenes.title: The End
scenes.summary: Lessons, rhymes, a village that will not explain itself, and a scream on a platform; then the narrator declines to follow the father through the door.

characters.name: Roberta (Bobbie)
characters.role: The eldest child; the one who is told
characters.summary: She is eleven at the start and twelve by her birthday, and her distinguishing gift is tact, more than courage: she works out early that her mother is unhappy, decides not to find out why, and goes on deciding it for ten chapters. When the newspaper hands her the answer she carries it alone, which makes her the only child in the book living in the adult world and the only one who cannot say so.
characters.clue: She tears up her petticoat for flags, faints across the line with them still in her hands, and afterwards can only say that they never got any cherries.

characters.name: Peter
characters.role: The middle child, aged ten at the start; would be an engineer
characters.summary: He is the one who acts and then works out afterwards whether he was right. He takes coal from the station heap on a fine distinction between mining and stealing, goes back to apologise when the distinction collapses, and later knocks two shillings out of a signalman’s hand for offering them. His vanity is drawn exactly — he must have led the forlorn hope, and he must be told he is not a coward.
characters.clue: He explains to a Station Master that he is not a thief but a coal-miner, and is proud all his life of having told the truth with a bargee’s fingers tight on his ear.

characters.name: Phyllis
characters.role: The youngest; the one who means extremely well
characters.summary: Introduced in half a sentence as the child who meant extremely well, and kept to it: her bootlace is always undone, she upsets the lemonade, she crushes the clay nest she made. She is also the only one who forgives the signalman out loud, and the only one who says plainly that she was asking for the strawberries when Perks accuses her of it, because she knows she will not like herself otherwise.
characters.clue: She is told she is ungentlemanly and cries about it on the railway line; she also tells a man who has just tried to buy her silence that she forgives him.

characters.name: Mother
characters.role: The children’s mother; a writer of stories by necessity
characters.summary: She is never given a name and is the most controlled figure in the book. She laughs while she is tucking Peter up on the drawing-room sofa on the last night in the old house, writes all day to buy the mutton, will not let the children accept a stranger’s hamper, and tells them nothing. Her one slip is the sentence about English judges thinking a man has done wrong, said to three children who do not know that a jury has just thought it of their father.
characters.clue: She lights fourteen candles in an empty dining-room because nobody can be cheerful in the dark except owls and dormice, and is found later with her head on her arms on the table.

characters.name: Father
characters.role: A clerk in a Government Office, convicted of selling State secrets
characters.summary: He is present for one evening and one chapter: mending a toy engine, telling his daughters that girls are as clever as boys, joking about moats and drawbridges. Then he is a cab door closing. Everything afterwards reaches the reader at second or third hand — an unopened trunk of his clothes, a name in a newspaper column, a letter that does not arrive — until he walks off the 11.54 with his lips set in a thin close line.
characters.clue: He can mend a rocking-horse, a doll’s cradle and the beasts from a Noah’s Ark, and he spends spring and summer looking at flagstones and gravel and a little grudging grass.

characters.name: Albert Perks
characters.role: The porter at the station; thirty-two, married, three children
characters.summary: He answers questions beginning with ‘Why’, which people in higher ranks of life often seem weary of, and he is the book’s sharpest instrument for measuring class. He is offended when the children keep the Russian’s story from him, and far more offended by a heap of birthday presents, because a man who has kept out of debt on a porter’s wages cannot afford to be an object of charity in his own village.
characters.clue: He makes tea in a beer can, gave up keeping his birthday before the children were born, and has something else to keep instead — the kids and the missus.
traits: sure that one must take a side

characters.name: The old gentleman
characters.role: A daily passenger on the 9.15; a director of the railway
characters.summary: He is never named, by the children or by the narrator, who keeps that as the one secret the book will not give up. He waves back, sends a hamper, finds an exile’s family, gives three gold watches and, without being asked, starts looking into a conviction he had doubted when he read about it. His power is money and acquaintance, and Nesbit lets him use both without ever making a speech about either.
characters.clue: His collars are an odd shape and his hat is not quite like other people’s; he tells every passenger at his own station to look out of the window that morning.

characters.name: The Russian gentleman (Szezcpansky)
characters.role: A writer imprisoned and exiled for a book about the poor
characters.summary: He arrives without a ticket, without English, and without any idea where in England his wife and children are. Three years in a dungeon, a chained march to Siberia, the mines for life, and a desertion during the war have left him crying at a country station. The children’s mother tells his story to her own children with the word Russia doing a great deal of work, and none of them notices what it is standing in for.
characters.clue: He is identified by a stamp, dressed in another man’s night-shirt, and cries out once in the garden in a way that makes a girl’s heart leap and then tremble.

characters.name: Jim
characters.role: A schoolboy from Maidbridge; the hound in the red jersey
characters.summary: He trips on a wire in the tunnel, breaks his leg, and is carried up to Three Chimneys because Bobbie is certain her mother would want it. His arrival converts the house into a hospital and his grandfather’s money into a cook, a housemaid and a rest for a woman who has been writing to feed three children. He is also, at first, the only person in the book who does not know anything about the family.
characters.clue: He hates all pawings, and asks a girl he has just met to hold his hand because the candle has to be put out.

characters.name: The Station Master
characters.role: Mr Gills, who keeps the station and the inner temple behind the ticket window
characters.summary: He catches Peter on the coal heap in a pair of old seaside sand shoes, tells him that stealing is stealing, and then lets him go and never mentions it again. He is the local representative of authority throughout — official with a crowd, doubtful about a foreigner without a ticket, formal about affairs of State — and he is also the man who wrings Bobbie’s hand like a pump-handle on the last morning without explaining why.
characters.clue: He waits like a cat by a mousehole in the shadow of a brake-van, and afterwards is jolly with the culprits just as if coal had never been discovered.

characters.name: Dr W. W. Forrest
characters.role: The village doctor, and rather a poor one himself
characters.summary: He orders grapes, beef essence and the best brandy for a patient who cannot pay for any of it, and when Bobbie asks whether the family can join a club like Mrs Viney’s he agrees to invent one. He is also the man who takes Peter for a walk and explains, as science, that girls are softer and weaker and must be handled carefully — a speech the novel has already contradicted twice and will contradict again.
characters.clue: He weeds his pansy-bed in his shirt sleeves, threatens to send a bill as long as the aqueduct, and calls the eldest child Lady Grave-airs.

themes.name: What the children are not told
themes.summary: At the centre of the novel is a fact kept from three children, from two of them to the last page, and from the reader for two thirds of the book. Nesbit does not merely delay the information; she makes the withholding itself the action, so that tact, silence and the decision not to ask become the things her characters actually do.
themes.development: The mother forbids questions in Chapter 1 and Bobbie immediately resolves not to know she has been crying; the unopened trunk of a man’s clothes in Chapter 5 is almost too much for her; the newspaper gives her the answer in Chapter 10; and in Chapter 11 the mother asks whether Bobbie will tell the others, hears ‘Because—’, and says ‘Exactly’, which is the whole book in one word.

themes.name: Verdicts, and who listens
themes.summary: Three people in this book are punished for things they did not do, or did not do in the way the charge says: a Russian writer sent to the mines for a book about the poor, a father convicted on letters somebody else put in his desk, and a boy who believes he has been mining, not stealing. Nesbit is careful to show that the machinery of judgement is the same in each case, and that only influence moves it.
themes.development: A Station Master decides privately to look over one case; the mother explains that English judges only think a man has done wrong; she says bitterly that nobody will listen to her; and what finally works is a rich acquaintance who had doubts when he read the papers, not a legal appeal.

themes.name: Playing at being Poor
themes.summary: The family’s poverty is real enough to mean jam or butter but not both, and unreal enough to be reversible, and Nesbit knows the difference better than her children do. The book’s hardest chapter sets their idea of a kind present against a porter’s idea of what a man loses when the village decides he cannot make both ends meet.
themes.development: The pretty furniture is left behind and the useful furniture packed; Peter takes coal because they cannot afford a fire; the children are forbidden to ask strangers for things and go on doing it for other people; and Perks makes them read out every label before he will accept a bun.

themes.name: Wages, hours and the people who keep the line
themes.summary: Nesbit’s railway is a workplace before it is a playground, and almost everyone the children love is somebody at work: a porter cleaning lamps, an engine-driver explaining the injector, a signalman who has not slept in five days because his son has pneumonia and nobody can be found to take his duty. The mother’s writing is put on the same footing — so many pages, so many buns.
themes.development: The whitewash line on the coal heap is there because coal gets stolen; Perks is paid in respect as well as wages; the signalman’s exhaustion is a staffing failure, not a moral one; and the book’s comfortable ending is partly a woman being able to stop writing for money.

themes.name: Three Chimneys
themes.summary: A house that is first a dark lump with no supper in it becomes the place where a stranger is put to bed in another man’s night-shirt and an injured boy is carried in without anyone being asked. Nesbit measures the family’s recovery by how much of the house they can give away, and she ends the novel on a threshold, not inside.
themes.development: The arrival by candlelight; the forgotten room with the cold beef in it; the Russian in the chair that had been the father’s; the hospital with one patient; and the last page, where the narrator stands outside the back door and then walks off across the field.

themes.name: The railway as a living thing
themes.summary: The trains are named like beasts, spoken to, waved at and thanked, and the children’s affection for them is treated as a real relationship, not a childish mistake. What keeps this from being whimsy is that Nesbit also gives the machine its technical vocabulary — couplings, injector, automatic brake, the communication cord — so the dragon and the engine are the same object seen twice.
themes.development: The 9.15 becomes the Green Dragon and the tunnel its lair; Bobbie is taught the brake by the driver she has frightened; the train she stops seems almost to have heard her; and on the last morning the whole train answers, which is the only moment the book lets the fancy come true.

themes.name: Friendliness, not charity
themes.summary: The children make friends across every line the period draws — a porter, a bargee, a doctor, a schoolboy, a director of the railway — and the book is unusually precise about what makes such a friendship possible and what breaks it. What matters is less the generosity than whether the person on the receiving end can accept without being diminished.
themes.development: Peter apologises on a lonely road to a man who has caught him stealing; Perks is angrier at being pitied than at being ignored; a bargeman who has twisted Peter’s ear gives the children the freedom of nineteen locks; and a clergyman supplies the word the book wants, loving-kindness.

themes.name: A narrator who will not stay out of it
themes.summary: The story is told by someone who interrupts it. She admits preferences, addresses the reader, changes a character’s name because she has tired of the longer one, and says plainly when she is keeping something back. The children’s ignorance of their father is held in place by a teller who knows and chooses her moment.
themes.development: The aside on Roberta’s name in Chapter 2 gives the eldest child two names, and the book uses both: Bobbie to her family, Roberta when she turns on herself. Later the narrator steps in to say what she will not describe, so that the reunion at the station is given in a few words and left to the reader.

techniques.name: The gap where the fact should be
techniques.definition: What the narrative declines to show, placed where the reader will notice the gap and fill it.
techniques.inThisBook: The arrest happens behind a library door; the trial happens between chapters; the prison is never entered. Nesbit puts the reader inside the children’s ignorance and then leaves clues only they would miss — a trunk of men’s clothes that have not gone with their owner, a mother who posts her own letters, a bitter aside about English judges. The reader solves it a page or two before Bobbie does, which is exactly the margin the book wants.

techniques.name: The narrator who talks to you
techniques.definition: A narrator or speaker turning outward to address the reader or the audience by name.
techniques.inThisBook: ‘I don’t suppose they had ever thought about railways’ is the second sentence, and the narrator never afterwards pretends to be absent. She admits she is growing fond of Roberta, drops the name Roberta because nobody else uses it, calls you the Gentle Reader when the subject is priggishness, and at the end tells you that you and she are not wanted in the house and had better go. The device makes a confidante of the reader, which is why the withheld secret is so uncomfortable.

techniques.name: The returning phrase
techniques.definition: A phrase brought back at intervals, so that its meaning shifts with what has happened since.
techniques.inThisBook: ‘All prisoners and captives’ is said three times in one paragraph by a mother who cannot say why, and comes back in Bobbie’s letter as ‘She told us once to pray for all prisoners and captives. I see now.’ The daily cry of ‘Take our love to Father’ works the same way: a game in Chapter 3, and in the last chapter a message that has, without anyone knowing it, been going to the right address.

techniques.name: Objects that carry the plot
techniques.definition: An object the narrative comes back to until it stands for the argument itself.
techniques.inThisBook: A toy engine bursts in Chapter 1 and is mended by a stranger in Chapter 4, which is the whole plot in miniature. Two red flannel petticoats become six flags; a sheet of newspaper round a parcel of magazines becomes the verdict; three gold watches are offered and Bobbie proposes selling them to find somebody else’s wife. Nesbit prefers to let a household object do the work a speech would otherwise have to do.

techniques.name: The set piece
techniques.definition: A self-contained episode built to a single effect and complete in itself, whether comic or ceremonial.
techniques.inThisBook: The landslide, the birthday tea, the burning barge, the tunnel: each occupies a chapter, has its own shape and could be read aloud on its own, which is what serial publication in thirteen monthly parts asks for. The device has a cost — the chapters can be shuffled in the memory — and Nesbit offsets it by threading the father’s absence through every one of them.

techniques.name: Dialect
techniques.definition: Spelling and grammar used to mark where a speaker comes from, and what being heard that way costs them.
techniques.inThisBook: Perks, Mrs Viney, Bill the Bargee, the engine-driver and the signalman are written phonetically; the family and the old gentleman are not. The spelling is therefore a map of who is being listened to, and the book notices it more than once: a porter is surprised that anyone answers his questions, and the same porter has to be shown written labels before he will believe his neighbours respect him.

techniques.name: Foils and doubles
techniques.definition: A character constructed to throw another’s choices into relief by making different ones.
techniques.inThisBook: The Russian is the father with the lid off: a man imprisoned for something he wrote, separated from a wife and children who do not know where he is. He arrives in Chapter 5, wears the father’s clothes, sits in the father’s chair, and is restored to his family nine chapters before the father is. The three children are graded the same way — Bobbie who knows, Peter who acts, Phyllis who says the thing out loud.

quotations.text: They were not railway children to begin with.
quotations.context: The novel’s first sentence.
quotations.analysis: The title is contradicted before the reader has finished the first line, and the tense does the work: were not, to begin with, implies a middle and an end already known to the teller. It also warns that the railway is something that happened to these children, not something they are, which is the difference between this book and an adventure story about trains.

quotations.text: “Of course they can. Girls are just as clever as boys, and don't you forget it! How would you like to be an engine-driver, Phil?”
quotations.speaker: Father
quotations.context: Peter has asked doubtfully whether girls can help to mend engines; his father is taking the toy apart on the table.
quotations.analysis: This is almost the last thing the father says before the knock at the door, and Nesbit puts it where it will be remembered. It licenses everything the girls do afterwards — the petticoat flags, the ride in the cab, the nursing in the tunnel — and it sets up the novel’s one real disagreement with itself, when Dr Forrest explains to Peter, as science, that girls are softer and weaker and have to be.

quotations.text: “Father's been called away--on business,” said Mother. “Come, darlings, go at once.”
quotations.speaker: Mother
quotations.context: The two gentlemen have gone, a cab has driven away, and she has come back into the room with her face as white as her lace collar.
quotations.analysis: The dash is the arrest. Everything before it is true and everything after it is a formula, and the pause in the middle is the only sign that a sentence is being assembled, not spoken. Nesbit will keep this trick going for nine chapters: nothing said to the children is a lie, and nothing said to them is the truth either.

quotations.text: “If Mother doesn't want us to know she's been crying,” she said to herself as she heard through the dark the catching of her Mother's breath, “we WON'T know it. That's all.”
quotations.speaker: Bobbie
quotations.context: Their mother has come up late to kiss the sleeping children, and only Bobbie has woken.
quotations.analysis: Knowing is turned into something a child can decide to do or not do, which is a strange and precise idea to give an eleven-year-old, and the capitals on WON’T are the italics of a vow. Note the plural: we won’t know it. Bobbie appoints herself the keeper of a silence the other two have not been asked about, and she will keep it, alone, for the whole book.

quotations.text: “We're taking the useful ones,” said Mother; “we've got to play at being Poor for a bit, my chickabiddy.”
quotations.speaker: Mother
quotations.context: Bobbie has noticed that the beautiful inlaid cabinet is being left behind and that they seem to be taking all the ugly things.
quotations.analysis: Play at, for a bit, and a nursery endearment: three softenings in one short sentence, and the capital P on Poor makes poverty a part in a game, not a condition. The children take her at her word — Mother had told them more than once that they were quite poor now, but this did not seem to be anything but a way of speaking — and it takes three wet days in June and a refused fire to teach them otherwise.

quotations.text: “Oh!” said Roberta, drawing a long breath; “it was like a great dragon tearing by. Did you feel it fan us with its hot wings?”
quotations.speaker: Roberta
quotations.context: The children’s first close sight of a train, from the top of the fence at the bottom of the field, the morning after they arrive.
quotations.analysis: The simile is the child’s, not the narrator’s, and it is allowed to stand, uncorrected, as a description of a real machine. Everything the book later does with the railway grows from here: the 9.15 becomes the Green Dragon, the tunnel becomes its lair, and Phyllis decides in the dark of Chapter 11 that a train takes its own shape in there. Nesbit never says the children are wrong; she simply also teaches them what an injector is.

quotations.text: I am tired of calling Roberta by her name. I don't see why I should. No one else did. Everyone else called her Bobbie, and I don't see why I shouldn't.
quotations.context: An aside in brackets, dropped into the middle of a conversation about toy engines.
quotations.analysis: A narrator announcing that she has got bored of her own formality is a small joke, but it changes the book. From here the eldest child has two names, and Nesbit uses the split: Bobbie is the girl her family sees, Roberta the one she addresses when she is angry with herself in the tunnel. The aside also establishes that this teller will interrupt, admit preferences and keep back whatever she likes.

quotations.text: Well, it was just like that with the sorrow the children had felt at Father's going away, and at Mother's being so unhappy. It made a deep impression, but the impression did not last long.
quotations.context: The end of a long comparison with a finger poked into a crock of dough set by the fire to rise.
quotations.analysis: The simile is domestic, slightly greedy and entirely unsentimental, and it says the thing most books for children will not: that the young forget, and that the forgetting is elastic and healthy, not callous. It is also a piece of housekeeping. Nesbit needs her children cheerful for eight chapters of larks, and this paragraph buys them without pretending the grief was shallow.

quotations.text: “I'm not a thief,” said Peter, as firmly as he could. “I'm a coal-miner.”
quotations.speaker: Peter
quotations.context: The Station Master has come out of the dark in a pair of old seaside sand shoes and taken him by the collar on top of the coal heap.
quotations.analysis: Peter’s defence is a real argument — he has reasoned that the outside of the heap might be stealing and the middle only mining — and he is brave enough to make it while being held by the jacket. The Station Master’s reply is the book’s plainest sentence about property: stealing is stealing, and what’s mine isn’t yours, whether you call it mining or whether you don’t. Eight chapters later a jury will decide what to call something a different man did not do.

quotations.text: He was a very nice-looking old gentleman, and he looked as if he were nice, too, which is not at all the same thing.
quotations.context: The first description of the passenger in the first-class carriage who waves back at the children.
quotations.analysis: A whole theory of appearances in eleven words, and one of the few moments where Nesbit’s adult irony is aimed at her adult reader over the children’s heads. The distinction matters later: this is a book in which a man’s good looks and good standing are what finally get another man out of prison, and the narrator has taken care to note that the two things are usually confused.

quotations.text: neither her own children nor you nor any other children in the world could ever understand exactly what it cost her to do it. Only some few of you, like Bobbie, may understand a very little bit.
quotations.context: Their mother has just given the children permission to walk on the railway line, having admitted that she did it herself as a girl.
quotations.analysis: The sentence turns from the story to the person holding the book and sorts them: most of you cannot understand this, a few of you can. It is a considerable thing to say to a child reader, and it identifies the quality the book values above bravery — the capacity to notice what an adult is paying. Bobbie is named as the type of it, which is why the narrator can later say, without embarrassment, that she is growing fond of her.

quotations.text: it's quite true that we're poor, but we have enough to live on. You mustn't go telling everyone about our affairs--it's not right. And you must never, never, never ask strangers to give you things.
quotations.speaker: Mother
quotations.context: The children have owned up to the letter and the hamper, and she has been angrier than they have ever known her, and then cried, and then apologised for being angry.
quotations.analysis: Two prohibitions are folded together here and only one of them is about money. Telling everyone about our affairs is the rule that governs the entire book, and it is being laid down by a woman whose own affairs include a husband in prison. The three nevers are the give-away: this is a household under siege, well beyond household economy, and the children take away only the part about hampers.

quotations.text: “Or when the Judges THINK they've done wrong,” said Mother. “Yes, that's so in England. But in Russia it was different.”
quotations.speaker: Mother
quotations.context: Peter has objected that people only go to prison when they have done wrong; his mother is explaining why a Russian writer was sent to Siberia.
quotations.analysis: The most exposed sentence in the novel, and the children walk straight past it. She corrects her son’s idea of justice, concedes that the correction applies to England, and then covers the concession with a contrast that lets her go on talking about somewhere else. The capitals mark the stress she puts on THINK; the full stop after England is where her own case is, and she steps over it.

quotations.text: “Yes,” said Mother, “upon all prisoners and captives. All prisoners and captives.”
quotations.speaker: Mother
quotations.context: Bobbie has repeated the phrase back to her to check that she has it right, at the end of the evening the Russian arrives.
quotations.analysis: The words come from the litany, where they are safely general, and the mother is using the form of a prayer to say something she cannot say in her own voice. The repetition is the point: she says it once as instruction and once as her own petition, and the second time there is nobody in the sentence but her husband. Bobbie will quote it back in a letter six chapters later with the three words that close the circle — I see now.

quotations.text: “I--I don't know,” said Bobbie, angry with herself, but still clinging to that resolution of hers, not to see anything that Mother didn't mean her to see.
quotations.context: She has found her father’s clothes in the locked black trunk, worked out that he cannot have taken them with him, and blurted out a question about whether he is dead.
quotations.analysis: Not to see is a remarkable formulation, since she has already seen; what she is refusing is the inference. Nesbit is describing a discipline, not an innocence, and what it costs Bobbie is in the phrase angry with herself. This is the technique of the whole novel stated as a character trait: the evidence is lying open in the room, and the decision is not to read it.

quotations.text: “Well, you see, you must take one side or the other. Same as with Liberals and Conservatives. The great thing is to take your side and then stick to it, whatever happens.”
quotations.speaker: Perks
quotations.context: Perks has been asked why he is on the side of the Japanese, having just agreed that the Russian government’s treatment of the exile was wicked.
quotations.analysis: This is the book’s only sustained piece of political comedy, and it is sharper than it looks. Perks has already said that the Station Master kept the story quiet because a man’s got to stand up for his own side whatever they does, and that foreigners are all tarred with the same brush. Taking a side and sticking to it is precisely what the jury in the father’s case has done, and Nesbit lets a porter explain the mechanism without once mentioning the trial.

quotations.text: “We never got any cherries, after all,” said Bobbie.
quotations.speaker: Bobbie
quotations.context: Walking home from the station after the cheering, while Peter and Phyllis congratulate themselves on having saved the train.
quotations.analysis: The others think her rather heartless, and the narrator lets that judgement stand for a chapter before explaining that Bobbie wakes screaming for months afterwards. The line is a small masterpiece of displacement: she cannot talk about the trustful engine rushing towards the mound, so she talks about fruit. It is the same manoeuvre her mother makes with Russia, learned from her without either of them noticing.

quotations.text: It just means that a person is able to know that you are unhappy, and to love you extra on that account, without bothering you by telling you all the time how sorry she is for you.
quotations.context: The narrator, having admitted that she is growing fond of Roberta, explains what is meant by the power of silent sympathy.
quotations.analysis: The definition is given in the plainest possible words and then undercut by the admission that follows it: this needs practice, it is not so easy as you might think. What is being praised is a skill, not a temperament, and the novel is unusual in treating tact as an achievement of the same order as stopping a train. The whole passage is addressed to you, so the reader is being taught as well as told.

quotations.text: “Oh, yes,” said Bobbie; “I think everyone in the world is friends if you can only get them to see you don't want to be UN-friends.”
quotations.speaker: Bobbie
quotations.context: The end of the barge day, after a man who twisted Peter’s ear has taken them the whole trip to Farley and back. Her mother answers, ‘Perhaps you’re right’, and sighs.
quotations.analysis: Nesbit gives her heroine the book’s most hopeful proposition and then puts an adult sigh immediately after it, which is the most efficient piece of undercutting in the novel. Bobbie’s rule has worked on a bargee, a porter and a Station Master; it has not worked on a jury, and her mother knows it. The coined word UN-friends is the giveaway that this is still a child’s formulation.

quotations.text: “I think,” said the clergyman, “it was what is sometimes called loving-kindness.”
quotations.speaker: The clergyman
quotations.context: Mrs Perks, going round the village to thank everyone, has asked whether what the children did was friendliness.
quotations.analysis: For twenty pages the chapter has kept the word charity at bay — Perks will not have it, his wife says nobody would offer it to him, and the children did not mean it — so the right word has to be found by somebody with a professional vocabulary. Loving-kindness is a translation of a biblical term for covenant faithfulness, which is heavier than the tea-table it is used at; Nesbit slips in the one register in which a gift between unequals is not a humiliation.

quotations.text: The name of the man who had been tried was the name of her Father. The verdict was 'Guilty.' And the sentence was 'Five years' Penal Servitude.'
quotations.context: Bobbie has stopped at the level-crossing with a parcel of Perks’s old magazines and idly read the newspaper it is wrapped in.
quotations.analysis: Three flat sentences, each a fact from a legal record, and the shock comes from the machinery of citation, not from any emotion. The formula the name of the man was the name of her Father is exact: she is reading about a stranger until the last three words. Nesbit has arranged for the truth to arrive as waste paper, wrapped round a kindness done by a porter, and the bottom of the column is torn off.

quotations.text: “Are you going to tell the others?” Mother asked. “No.” “Why?” “Because--” “Exactly,” said Mother; “so you understand why I didn't tell you. We two must help each other to be brave.”
quotations.context: Bobbie has brought the cutting to her mother’s room and locked the door.
quotations.analysis: The reason is never given, by either of them, and the novel’s whole method is justified in a word and a half. Bobbie starts an explanation, finds she does not need one, and the trailing dash is accepted as an argument; the silence that has looked for ten chapters like evasion is revealed as the same choice the daughter has just made unprompted. It also promotes her: they are now two adults with a secret, no longer a mother and a child.

quotations.text: “Nobody will listen,” said Mother, very bitterly, “nobody at all. Do you suppose I've not tried everything?
quotations.speaker: Mother
quotations.context: Bobbie has just suggested explaining to the lawyers about the jealous subordinate who got her father’s place.
quotations.analysis: Very bitterly is the only such adverb attached to this character in the book, and it is earned. She has the explanation, she has the suspect, and she has no standing; the letters she writes to Members of Parliament and Editors of papers on a stranger’s behalf in Chapter 6 were presumably written on her husband’s behalf first. What eventually moves the case is a railway director who happens to know some Russians and to read the papers carefully, more than any evidence.

quotations.text: “SILLY little girl!” said Roberta to Bobbie, and felt better.
quotations.context: Alone in the tunnel with an unconscious boy, she has cut away his stocking, seen the broken leg and felt the ground go unsteady.
quotations.analysis: The two names are now two people, and the sterner one is put in charge. Nesbit explains in the next paragraph that Bobbie hates being called a little girl by anybody, even kindly, and allows Roberta to do it only when she is very angry with herself — so the insult is also a private joke and a way of standing up. It is the same machinery as her mother’s bravery, seen from inside and at eleven years old.

quotations.text: “Yes,” she said, “I do believe it--almost always--except when I'm so sad that I can't believe anything. But even when I can't believe it, I know it's true--and I try to believe. You don't know how I try, Peter.
quotations.speaker: Mother
quotations.context: Peter has asked whether she really believes what she has just said about being characters in a book that God is writing.
quotations.analysis: A book for children that lets a mother admit she cannot always believe her own consolation is doing something unusual, and the three dashes are the hesitation written into the punctuation. The distinction she draws — I know it’s true and I try to believe — is the same distinction Bobbie makes between seeing and allowing oneself to have seen. It is also the closest the novel comes to saying out loud how tired she is.

quotations.text: “Oh! my Daddy, my Daddy!” That scream went like a knife into the heart of everyone in the train, and people put their heads out of the windows to see a tall pale man with lips set in a thin close line, and a little girl clinging to him with arms and legs, while his arms went tightly round her.
quotations.context: Three people get off the 11.54: a countryman with chickens, the grocer’s wife’s cousin, and the third.
quotations.analysis: Nesbit holds back from the close-up. The reunion is shown from the carriage windows, at the distance of strangers, so that the reader is given the sound and then the picture other people see; the father is a tall pale man before he is anybody’s father, and his set lips record ten months that the book has declined to describe. It is the loudest moment in a novel that has been quiet on purpose, and it lasts one sentence.

quotations.text: I think we will not open the door or follow him. I think that just now we are not wanted there. I think it will be best for us to go quickly and quietly away.
quotations.context: The novel’s last paragraph. The father has gone in and the door has shut behind him.
quotations.analysis: The narrator who has interrupted, teased and confided for fourteen chapters closes by withholding one more thing, and this time names the reason. Three sentences beginning I think give the decision the feel of a judgement made on the spot, not a device prepared in advance. The book that is about what may properly be kept from people ends by keeping its own reunion from the reader, and walks off across the field.

timeline.label: Edith Nesbit born in London
timeline.detail: The daughter of an agricultural chemist who died when she was three; the family moved often afterwards, in England and on the Continent.

timeline.label: The family settles at Halstead in Kent
timeline.detail: For about three years, in a house beside the railway. Nesbit wrote warmly about the place in later life, and it is usually identified as a model for the country of this novel, though nothing in the book names a county.

timeline.label: Marriage to Hubert Bland
timeline.detail: Their son Paul, born the same year, is the boy to whom The Railway Children is dedicated for his knowledge of railways.

timeline.label: The Fabian Society is founded
timeline.detail: Bland was a founder member and its first treasurer, and Nesbit wrote and spoke for it. The politics of this novel — a writer jailed for a book about the poor, a signalman worked past exhaustion — belong to that household.

timeline.label: The Dreyfus case begins in France
timeline.detail: A French officer convicted of passing secrets to a foreign power on documents that were not his; the verdict was finally quashed in 1906. The parallel with the father’s case is close, and there is no evidence that Nesbit had any particular trial in mind.

timeline.label: The Story of the Treasure Seekers, and the move to Well Hall
timeline.detail: Her first great success with the Bastable children, and the move to the moated house at Eltham, then in Kent, where she lived for more than twenty years and where this novel was written.

timeline.label: The Russo-Japanese War
timeline.detail: Fought from February 1904 to September 1905. It is the war the Russian exile deserts from, and the reason Perks has taken the Japanese side by the time the children meet him.

timeline.label: Serialisation in The London Magazine
timeline.detail: Thirteen monthly instalments from January 1905, which is why the chapters are so nearly self-contained. The watches the children are given are engraved with the year 1905, the only date the story puts on itself.

timeline.label: Published as a book
timeline.detail: By Wells Gardner, Darton and Co., with twenty black-and-white plates by C. E. Brock, including the frontispiece.

timeline.label: Nesbit dies in Kent
timeline.detail: At New Romney, having published some forty books for children as well as poetry, novels and ghost stories for adults.

timeline.label: A BBC television serial
timeline.detail: The last of several BBC versions, with Jenny Agutter as Bobbie; it was made in the studio and largely without trains.

timeline.label: Lionel Jeffries’s film
timeline.detail: Filmed on the Keighley and Worth Valley Railway in West Yorkshire, with Oakworth as the station, Jenny Agutter again as Bobbie and Bernard Cribbins as Perks. It fixed a Yorkshire setting on a book that never names one.

timeline.label: A television film for ITV
timeline.detail: Made on the Bluebell Railway in Sussex, with Jenny Agutter now playing the mother.

timeline.label: The Railway Children Return
timeline.detail: A sequel set among evacuees in 1944, bringing back Agutter as Bobbie and returning to Oakworth; evidence of how firmly the film’s Yorkshire has attached itself to the story.

places.name: London
places.note: The red-brick villa with every modern convenience, the Government Office where the father works, and the city the mother keeps going back to alone. The first page lists the children’s idea of it: Maskelyne and Cook’s, the Pantomime, the Zoological Gardens and Madame Tussaud’s.

places.name: Marlow, Buckinghamshire
places.note: The only place in England the novel names for the parents’ own past: Father and I used to go on the river at Marlow before we were married. The bargee’s wife names the same bridge as the site of the insult about the puppy-pie.

places.name: Halstead, Kent
places.note: Where Nesbit lived for about three years as a girl, in a house beside a railway. It is usually named as the model for the country of this book, and the identification rests on her own later affection for the place, not on anything in the novel, which gives its station no county and its railway an invented company.

places.name: Well Hall, Eltham
places.note: The moated house, then in Kent and now in south-east London, where Nesbit was living when the book was written and serialised.

places.name: Northumberland
places.note: Jim’s home, named once, when the farm bailiff asks where the boy with the broken leg lives. The point is the distance: it is why he is carried up to Three Chimneys instead.

places.name: Siberia
places.note: The mines the Russian was condemned to for life, reached on foot in a chain of convicts. The novel names nothing more exact than Siberia, and the coordinates here simply mark the middle of it.

places.name: Oakworth station, West Yorkshire
places.note: Not a place in the book. The station on the Keighley and Worth Valley Railway used for the 1970 film and again in 2022, and the reason most readers now picture the story in Yorkshire.

criticalViews.position: A novel about the management of knowledge
criticalViews.summary: On this reading the rescue chapters are the surface and the real subject is who is allowed to know what. The mother withholds; Bobbie discovers and then withholds in turn; the narrator withholds from the reader and closes by withholding the reunion. The book’s moral education is about tact, more than courage — the power of silent sympathy, defined in Chapter 7 as a skill that needs practice — and its most charged sentences are the ones in which a character almost says the thing and does not.
criticalViews.counter: The silence is also very convenient. Because nobody may ask questions, the novel never has to argue about whether the courts are trustworthy, and can resolve a miscarriage of justice through the private kindness of a rich acquaintance without examining what that implies.

criticalViews.summary: A sceptical account notes that the family’s hardship is genteel and temporary. They keep a charwoman throughout, their clothes are still nice, and the crisis is solved by a hamper, a benefactor and, at the end, a cook and a housemaid. Set beside the real poverty in the same pages — Mrs Viney’s twopence a week, the signalman with a sick child and no relief, Mrs Perks taking in washing — the children’s playing at being Poor can look like tourism.
criticalViews.counter: The novel says so itself, repeatedly and through its most sympathetic characters. Perks’s fury at the birthday presents is a whole chapter given over to exactly this objection, and it is he, not the children, who is allowed the last word on the difference between friendliness and charity.

criticalViews.position: A fairy tale that denies being one
criticalViews.summary: The plot depends on coincidence of a kind Nesbit elsewhere mocks: the stranger on the 9.15 turns out to be the injured boy’s grandfather and the man who can clear the father’s name. The narrator flags each one — things do happen in real life that are rather like books, sometimes; this is not a fairy story, and besides it really was four days and not three — which suggests a book conscious of having its cake and eating it, and covering itself with a joke.
criticalViews.counter: The flagging is the argument, not an excuse for it. Peter asks his mother to write a book in which Father comes home, and she answers that they are in a book God is writing; the coincidences belong to that frame, and the novel is candid that she cannot always believe it herself.

essayQuestions.question: ‘Because—’ ‘Exactly.’ How does Nesbit manage what the children, and the reader, are allowed to know?
essayQuestions.focus: Secrecy, tact and the withheld conviction
plan: Set out what is withheld and from whom: the arrest behind the library door, the trial between chapters, the sentence given once in a torn column, and Peter and Phyllis kept in the dark to the last page.
Show how the mother’s language works — called away on business, quite poor now, in Russia it was different — and note that none of it is a lie.

Track the clues Nesbit plants for the reader over the children’s heads: the trunk of unclaimed clothes, the letters posted only in town, the prayer for all prisoners and captives, the remark about what English judges think.
Examine Bobbie as the book’s theory of tact in practice, from ‘we WON’T know it’ in Chapter 1 to the resolution not to see anything her mother did not mean her to see.
Weigh the cost against the gain: what the silence protects the characters from, and what it also protects the novel from having to say.

essayQuestions.question: What does the Russian exile do for a book about an English family?
essayQuestions.focus: Doubling, political content and the uses of a foreign country
plan: Describe his story as the children hear it: a book about the poor, three years in a dungeon, the march to Siberia, a wife and children lost somewhere in England.
Line it up point by point against the father’s: a man imprisoned for something written, a family that does not know where he is, a wrong that nobody in authority will hear.
Consider the placement — he wears the father’s clothes and sits in the father’s chair, in the very chapter where Bobbie finds the trunk.
Read the mother’s account of Russian justice as a confession she can make only because it is about somewhere else, and ask what the contrast with England is doing.
Ask what is lost by keeping the politics foreign, and set Perks’s speech about taking a side beside it.

essayQuestions.question: Is the Perks birthday chapter a comic episode or the most serious thing in the novel?
essayQuestions.focus: Class, gifts and the difference between friendliness and charity
plan: Trace the plan from the hay-loft council to the pram, the gooseberries, the shovel and the fourteen buns marked A. P.
Set the children’s reasoning — we always have things on our birthdays — against Perks’s, that a man who has kept out of debt cannot be a laughing-stock in his own village.
Examine the turn: what moves him is the reading aloud of the labels, not an apology, and the labels make a gift into a record of what his neighbours think of him.
Consider the mother’s earlier warning that poor people are very proud, and whether the chapter agrees with her or improves on her.
Judge the clergyman’s word, loving-kindness, and decide whether it resolves the problem or renames it.

essayQuestions.question: How does Nesbit’s narrator change the book she is telling?
essayQuestions.focus: Direct address, asides and the refusal at the end
plan: Collect the intrusions: the candlestick-maker’s cart, the decision to stop calling Roberta by her name, the growing fondness for her, the Gentle Reader and the difficulty of not being a prig.
Show how the same voice sorts its readers — only some few of you, like Bobbie, may understand a very little bit — and what that does to a child reading it.
Look at the places where the narrator declines: the District Superintendent’s speech, the kind things Mrs Perks says, the old gentleman’s name, the reunion itself.
Consider whether the intimacy makes the withheld secret worse, since the reader has been treated throughout as a confidante.
Read the final paragraph closely and decide what the three sentences beginning ‘I think’ are claiming about the reader’s place in the story.

discussionQuestions: Peter and Phyllis never find out where their father has been. Is that a kindness, and is it the novel’s judgement or only their mother’s?
Peter argues that taking coal from the middle of the heap is mining, not stealing. Where else in the book does the name given to an act decide what it is?
The Russian’s imprisonment is described at length and the father’s is not described at all. What does Nesbit gain by that, and what does she avoid?
Perks would rather have no presents than be pitied. Do the children ever really understand his objection, or only get round it?
Dr Forrest tells Peter, as a scientific fact, that girls are softer and weaker. Which scenes in the novel are set against that speech, and does the book settle the question?

The old gentleman clears the father’s name because he happens to travel on the 9.15 and to read the papers carefully. How far does that ending undercut everything the novel has shown about who gets listened to?

related.why: Published two years later and the other great Edwardian book about a girl and the adults who will not explain themselves, with the same refusal to write down to its reader.
A close reading of a child insisting on her own name, to set beside Nesbit’s narrator deciding halfway through that Roberta shall be Bobbie.
A child, a convict and a benefactor who turns out to be somebody already met; Dickens sets his reunion at the centre of the book where Nesbit keeps hers off the page.
Dickens on prisons and who is owed pity, for comparison with the prayer for all prisoners and captives that a mother cannot explain.
Published two years later and the opposite experiment with the same Edwardian countryside: animals, a riverbank and a motor-car where Nesbit has children, a cutting and a timetable.
The suburban villa the children leave in the first chapter, described from the inside by a man who would die rather than let the neighbours know his affairs.
